# Best Way to Clean CV Joints of Old Grease

Removing old grease from Constant Velocity (CV) joints isn't just a matter of wiping surfaces clean; it is a critical preparation step that dictates the longevity and performance of your new boots. When you are about to replace CV boots, the goal is to expose the metal and rubber components to inspect for wear while creating a perfectly dry surface for the fresh lubricant to adhere to. Relying on throwaway rags alone often results in a contaminated workpiece that compromises the seal immediately upon reassembly.

The most effective solvent for this specific task is typically a dedicated degreaser or an automotive brake cleaner, provided it is formulated to evaporate without leaving residue. Common household solvents like acetone can be overly aggressive on certain rubber compounds and plastics found in modern drivetrain components, potentially causing swelling or cracking before you even finish cleaning. Brake cleaner is generally preferred because it dries instantly, reducing the window where dirt could settle back onto the surface. However, the choice of solvent matters less than the mechanical removal process that precedes it.

Before applying any chemical agent, a preliminary mechanical scrub is essential. Using a stiff-bristled brush or a dedicated degreasing cloth allows you to break down the bulk of the semi-solid grease. This step prevents excessive pooling of solvent and ensures that you aren't simply smearing old, contaminated grease around the joint. Once the bulk material is removed, apply your chosen cleaner liberally. Let it sit for a short duration to dissolve the remaining film, then scrub again with a fresh section of your cloth. The friction helps lift trapped debris from the raceways and snap rings, areas where old grease tends to accumulate most heavily.

After the solvent has done its work, allow the CV joint components to air dry completely. Rushing this step is a common pitfall; introducing moisture or residual solvent under a new boot can lead to premature failure of the seal lips. If you are working in an environment with high humidity, consider using compressed air to blow out any remaining liquid from the internal bearings and splines before wiping them down with a clean, lint-free rag.

Once dry, inspect the metal surfaces for pitting, corrosion, or scoring. Even if the old grease masked these issues, the new boot will only last as long as the underlying hardware allows. If you find significant damage, cleaning is no longer sufficient; replacement of the joint itself may be necessary.

If your vehicle is equipped with a modern transmission that uses electronic controls, ensure that no solvent mist drifts into sensitive sensors or connectors nearby. While brake cleaner is relatively safe, overspray can still affect optical sensors used for speed calculation in some architectures. Use targeted application methods to minimize risk.

Finally, before installing the new boots and filling them with fresh grease, verify that the snap rings are seated correctly. These small components often break or deform during disassembly, and old grease can hide cracks that aren't visible until it's too late. A clean inspection ensures you catch these failures immediately.
